messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Interior Designer
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 57

# The Weight of Walls

Marcus is a 67-year-old Māori man who has worked as an interior designer for nearly four decades. He lives alone in a modest home in Auckland, his wife of thirty-one years having passed from cancer three years ago. His children worry about him, though he tells them not to. He has always been, in his own words, a man who manages.

What happened to Marcus occurred seventeen years ago, during a contract job that took him to a remote region of Southeast Asia. He had been hired to consult on a resort development, a project that excited him — he had always believed that a well-designed space could restore a person. On his third day in the country, he was taken. A small group of armed men held him and two colleagues in a concrete outbuilding for twenty-two days. One of his colleagues was released after the first week. The other did not survive. Marcus was eventually freed following a negotiation he was never fully informed about. He flew home, told his wife he was fine, and returned to work within the month.

For years, he almost believed the story he told himself. He was busy. The work was meaningful. His wife was alive and the house was full of the particular noise that comes from a life shared with someone you love. He designed spaces for other people — chose colors that invited calm, arranged furniture to encourage conversation, selected lighting that made rooms feel safe. He was good at it. He still is.

But since his wife died, the architecture of his days has changed, and what he kept behind the walls has begun to find its way through.

He does not sleep well. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning with his heart hammering, certain, in those first terrible seconds, that the door is locked from the outside. He gets up and checks the locks — not once, but several times — and then sits in the kitchen under the brightest light he can stand until the feeling passes. He has replaced every dimmer switch in his house with standard fixtures. He cannot tolerate low light anymore. He tells clients it is an aesthetic preference.

He avoids enclosed spaces when he can manage it. He takes the stairs rather than lifts. He will not work in rooms without windows. When he cannot avoid a confined space — a storage room, a car park, a crowded elevator — something seizes in his chest and his mind goes somewhere else entirely, back to that concrete room, back to the smell of damp and rust and another man's fear. He has learned to excuse himself quickly and stand outside until the ground feels solid again.

He rarely speaks about what happened. He spoke to his wife once, briefly, in the early years, and her face changed in a way he did not want to cause again. Now there is no one he trusts with it. He sits with his grandchildren and watches them build things with blocks, and sometimes the sight of small enclosed structures — even toy ones — makes his stomach drop in a way he cannot explain to anyone in the room.

What troubles him most, he says, is not the fear itself but the way it has distorted his relationship to his work. He spent his career believing that space could be made safe, that a room could hold a person gently. He chose this work because he understood, instinctively, that where we live shapes how we feel. Now he moves through buildings with a different kind of knowledge — one that arrived in a locked room in the dark — and he cannot always separate the designer's eye from the survivor's dread. He looks at a beautiful room and part of him is already calculating the exits.

He is not sure, he says quietly, whether that ruins it or whether it has simply made him more honest about what walls can do.
